newsitem.title: USA: Illinois utility is biggest SO2 emitter.
newsitem.headline: Illinois utility is biggest SO2 emitter.

text.p: Illinova Corp's Illinois Power has the highest rate of sulfur dioxide emissions among the 50 largest utilities in the eastern United States, according to a study released Thursday.
The study ranking companies in terms of emissions per megawatt hour of power generated and tons per year was based on company emissions records supplied to the government.

For nitrogen oxide, TECO Energy Inc's Tampa Electric was the worst polluter based on emissions per unit of electricity generated. KU Energy Corp's Kentucky Utilities had the highest rate of carbon dioxide emissions.
By sheer volume, the largest polluters were Tennessee Valley Authority, American Electric Power Co, and Southern Company, the three largest generators in the eastern 37 states.
All of the biggest and heaviest polluters are largely dependent on coal burning for electricity.

The study by the Natural Resources Defense Council, New Jersey's Public Service Electric and Gas, and Pace University sought to let the public know which companies were the worst polluters, although all the utilities ranked were in compliance with U.S. emissions standards.
"They're not breaking the law," said NRDC senior attorney David Hawkins. "The law is inadequate."

He said as Congress and regulators sought to create a competitive electricity market nationwide, consumers who would soon have a choice of power suppliers should know exactly what they are buying, and Congress should ensure that all utilities were subject to the same pollution standards.
Under current law, coal-fired plants are subject to less stringent standards than other power plants.

"Everytime we turn on the light switch, we're not only getting light, we're getting dirt," Hawkins said at a news briefing. "It's about time to let the public know that there are some companies that sell you more dirt when they sell you electricity than others."
However, a spokesman for Cinergy Corp, one of the worst polluters on the ranking, said the study misunderstood how the deregulated market would work.
"We are growing considerably in our power marketing and trading. Of the electricity we're selling off of our system only 30 percent is coming from our own generation," said spokesman Steven Brash.

The study raised concern about sulfur dioxide emissions even though the Environmental Protection Agency's acid rain program has been widely praised for slashing SO2 emissions from power plants, the biggest source of the pollutant.
Under the program, the heaviest polluters have been allowed to buy emissions credits from other utilities which have cut their pollution more than required.
Nitrogen oxide emissions, which are also regulated, remain a problem, with Northeastern states concerned that pollution from coal-fired plants in the Midwest is blowing dirty air into their areas.

Tampa Electric said the study's index was "meaningless" because by ranking the company as the worst NOx emitter, the report failed to reflect that air quality in Florida meets federal smog standards and that in a recent preliminary review, EPA said Florida might not need any new NOx controls.
Owners of the coal-fired plants said they were not surprised by their rankings on carbon dioxide emissions, which are not regulated.

"If you're going to rank me on C02 emissions, and I'm coal fired, guess what, I'm going to be number one," said Caryl Pfeiffer, environmental affairs manager for Kentucky Utilities. An international agreement now under negotiation could force governments around the world to impose controls on carbon emissions.
